g318/sichuan.description: Day 1 of the trip. Reached Ya'an after a 130km ride from Chengdu.
An obelisk in Xingou, a small village in the mountains where I stayed overnight. The owner of the hostel is known among cyclists as a good cook.
After the Erlang Mountain Tunnel, the snow peaks are now visible in the distance.
Luding Bridge over the Dadu River, a significant historical site from the Long March of the Red Army. Behind it is the newly built expressway bridge.
Looking back before the tunnel. Road signs warning of slippery conditions, continuous downhill (which I just climbed up), and high traffic accident risk.
Kangding city at night, known for traditional folk songs.
Winding snowy roads going up to Zheduo Mountain Pass, the first high pass of the G318 at 4298m. It's said that anyone who can cycle up this pass can finish the whole G318 (not true).

Descending from Zheduo Mountain. The last few kilometres of climb to the top took me ages, and gave me a muscle injury so bad that I could barely walk that night. It was my first time cycling at such high altitude.
Grassland from Xinduqiao to Tagong, an 80km recovery ride. I ate dumplings halfway, which had to be cooked in a pressure cooker at this altitude.
Buddhist murals on rocks near Tagong.

Tagong Monastery. Local legend says that when Princess Wencheng was travelling to Tibet, the life-sized statue of a twelve-year-old Shakyamuni Buddha she was carrying became immovable here until a replica was left behind. Tibetans believe that if you cannot make the pilgrimage all the way to Lhasa, worshipping at Tagong Monastery yields the exact same spiritual merit.
Yala Snow Mountain.
A monastery on a small hill near where I stayed in Xinduqiao.
Yajiang's spiral overpass, a 300m vertical drop in just 8km (almost got scraped by a lorry here).
The 3000km road sign of the G318, filled with messages from cyclists. This stretch is the steepest 10km of the journey, averaging about 9-10% gradient.
Three Sisters Hostel at Xiangkezong, a well-known pit stop for cyclists, motorcyclists, and backpackers. Its walls are filled with messages left by travellers.
Me after climbing up the Eighteen Bends of the Sky Road (天路十八弯). Now 4000m is the baseline altitude I'm cycling at.
Yak sign on the way to Litang.
Changqingchun Ke'er Monastery under the afternoon sun.
Yaks on Maoya Grassland.
Messages left behind by travellers on the wall of a hostel in Heni.
Newly paved roads.
Fellow cyclist near the top of Haizi Mountain, 4685m above sea level.
One of the best views of the trip.

g318/tibet.description: Motorists and cyclists on the Jinsha River (upper Yangtze) Bridge, officially entering Tibet.
On top of Zongla Mountain. This was one of the toughest days of the entire trip, with a 1700m climb over 105km.
Weise Monastery, over 580 years old.
The Nu River Bridge. Nu literally means 'angry', reflecting its turbulent nature.
Upper Rawu Lake.
Lower Rawu Lake. This is known as the most scenic ride of the G318 route.
The snow peaks look surprisingly low and close.
One of the best things about a bicycle is that you can stop anywhere without obstructing traffic.
Midui Glacier in the distance. The yellowish glacier-fed stream is merging with the turquoise Parlung Tsangpo River.
Beginning the ride in yet more rain.
Tongmai was once one of the most dangerous stretches of the G318, where rain made landslides frequent. Modern bridges and tunnels have since made it much safer.
Lulang's alpine meadows.
Coldest ride of the trip. Got soaked on the climb to Sejila Mountain Pass, 4728m above sea level.
Me at the Nyang River, known as the mother river of Nyingchi.
Lhasa-Nyingchi Expressway beside the G318.

Last climb to Mila Mountain Pass. At this exact point I had to stop due to a sharp chest pain. Looking back, my cardiopulmonary system had been severely overloaded over the past week, and I should have taken one or two rest days.
5013m above sea level - the highest point I have ever reached on a bicycle.
A statue of Songtsen Gampo, the seventh-century ruler who unified Tibet.
The Lhasa River.

The Jokhang Temple, the spiritual centre of Tibet for more than 1300 years and the finish point of the G318 pilgrimage. It was built in the seventh century under the reign of Songtsen Gampo. Its most sacred treasure is the Jowo Shakyamuni statue, said to have been made during the lifetime of Shakyamuni Buddha, depicting him at the age of twelve, and brought to Tibet by Princess Wencheng of the Tang Dynasty.

The Potala Palace, whose White Palace historically served as the Dalai Lama's residence and the administrative centre of the Tibetan government. Inside the Red Palace, the reliquary stupa of the Fifth Dalai Lama is adorned with approximately 3.7 tonnes of gold and thousands of precious stones.
Nagenla Pass. My cycling was over, and I was fully enjoying the bus rides.
A white yak.
Namtso, meaning 'Heavenly Lake' in Tibetan, is one of Tibet's most sacred and spectacular alpine lakes.
Nyenchen Tanglha Mountains along the southern shores of Namtso.
Khata scarves on mani stone piles along the shores of Namtso.
Yamdrok Lake, meaning 'Turquoise Lake' in Tibetan, is another of Tibet's three great sacred lakes.
Yamdrok Lake. The railings are fully covered with khata scarves.

Rituo Monastery, a small Tibetan Buddhist monastery perched on a secluded peninsula stretching into the turquoise waters of Yamdrok Lake, often described as one of the loneliest monasteries in the world.
A wild fox near Rituo Monastery.
Another side of Yamdrok Lake.
Horses grazing near Yamdrok Lake.

triple-crown/hikes-city.description: Rainbow on the way to the airport.
Looking out over Lysefjord from Preikestolen.
At Kjeragbolten. It is a drop of almost 1000m to the fjord below.
Sheep on the way down from Kjerag.
Cute dog on the way down from Trolltunga.
The iconic row of wooden buildings at Bryggen.

xinjiang/duku.description: Packing my bicycle for the flight.
My belongings (many discarded later) laid out on the hotel bed.
Dushanzi Grand Canyon viewed from WJ's drone.

We were too excited and did not pace ourselves on the first day. With strong winds on top, we were so exhausted that we had to get off and push the bikes. You can see the Tianshan Mountains in the distance.
Our tent pitched in the car park of a hotel under construction at the Wusu tourism service area. None of us got up before 10am.

Sheep at Maoliugou outpost, where we spent the second night. AP crashed on the descent and badly hurt his knee, so we hitched a lorry back to Kuitun Hospital the next day. He was back on the bike for a 1900m climb the day after (absolutely crazy).
Starting the day with a 30km climb to Haxilegen Pass.
A braided river spreading across the valley.
The winding roads of Tianshan, and the steepest segment I have ever cycled to this day; the gradient never went below double digits (max gradient 39.6%).
Snow at Haxilegen Pass, 3400m above sea level, the highest point of our trip and my first time at altitudes above 3000m. Every breath felt noticeably thinner.
AP descending from Haxilegen Pass to Qiao'erma.
A small stream near Qiao'erma. This scene reminds me of the elven realms of Middle-earth.
Tangbula Grassland, where we did a chill recovery ride. None of us could take more climbs because of bruises (no one wore padded cycling shorts because I thought they were unnecessary...).
Our bikes parked at the roadside of Tangbula Grassland.
WJ (left) and AP (right) looking at the distant peaks.
Right before the tunnel of Yuximolegai Pass. We were soaked by the rain and had to wrap ourselves in emergency blankets. This was the closest I got to hypothermia.

Heavy fog and rain after Yuximolegai Tunnel. Despite poor visibility, we had to descend to lower, warmer altitudes. I was seriously considering calling the emergency helpline, but we rolled a die and it told us not to (we survived).
Sunset at Nalati Grassland after rain, fog, mud, and squeezing between heavy lorries in a big traffic jam.
My bike covered in mud. A good 20km of the road to Nalati town was under construction and full of mud and potholes. We had to stay put that day to wash and dry essentially everything.

xinjiang/ili.description: Centre of Tekes, the Bagua City. Officially a county-level city, though to me it feels more like a small but rather modern town.
Tekes at night. The city is laid out in the shape of the Taoist Bagua (Eight Trigrams), with roads radiating from the centre, so it needs no traffic lights.
Supper and drinks near a park south of the city centre, where we pitched our tent.
Officially entering Zhaosu County on the highway.
Crows along the highway to Zhaosu.
WJ (left) and AP (right) at the end of the Xiata Trail.
It was my first time seeing a proper snow peak. The silky deep greens, the white snow in the distance: you can almost feel the clarity of the air.
The last bit of lavender fields near Zhaosu, with snow-capped mountains in the distance.
Along the Yizhao Highway. You can see horses and sheep in the background.
Yizhao Highway's most exposed section, where the road is carved into the cliff.
Sunset after the steep descent. At this point, we could either pitch our tent by the roadside and sleep hungry, or cycle on to the city into the night.
Of course we chose to cycle till 1am. It was 70km of straight downhill: still one of the best rides ever.
WJ (left) and AP (right) at Sayram Lake.
It's said that Sayram Lake is the furthest point inland that moisture from the Atlantic reaches, hence its nickname, 'the last teardrop of the Atlantic'.
Every time I look back at this white rock, I somehow feel a sense of peace and calmness.
Packing our stuff to leave. This was the last stop of our trip, but our story has only just begun.
